passage: I ride the same bus as Sarika, so I noticed. Last Monday Sarika came out of the counsellor's room with a folded sheet. On it was a rough map: the back seats of the bus, the corridor by the science lab, the stairs near the gym, each marked with a red dot. By Wednesday Sarika was sitting in the front seats near the driver and the bus attendant, and walking the corridor with two friends. Someone had also given Sarika a small card with three names to go to quickly: the counsellor, the class teacher and the PT sir. On Thursday I saw Sarika glance back at the corridor and then keep walking. I don't know how Sarika feels. But Sarika didn't look as tense as last week. - Mridul

qa.q: What places were marked on the map Sarika carried?
qa.a: The back seats of the bus, the corridor by the science lab and the stairs near the gym.

qa.q: What might Sarika have been feeling, and how sure can Mridul be?
qa.a: Sarika may feel a bit safer, since Sarika looked less tense, though Mridul says plainly not knowing how Sarika feels.

qa.q: What else could Sarika and the counsellor add to the plan, and why?
qa.a: They could set a time to review how it is working, because places and people change and the plan should change with them.

qa.q: How might the two friends who walk with Sarika experience this?
qa.a: They probably feel useful and protective, glad to be trusted with a clear job.

grounding: The student, with a counsellor, identifies where the bullying occurs, such as the bus or corridor, and arranges to walk with friends, sit near the staff and know whom to approach quickly.

passage:
Day 1, Monday: In the counsellor's room, Arnab drew two circles on a paper. "The bus and the corridor near the Class 10 toilets. That's where it happens." Ms. Payal, the counsellor, nodded. "Let's plan for each spot."

Day 3, Wednesday: They had it written down. On the bus, Arnab would sit in the second seat, behind the driver, not the back. In the corridor, he'd walk with Irfan and Tenzing, who had agreed without a second's hesitation. If anything happened, he'd go straight to Mr. Saha, whose staffroom door was ten steps away. Ms. Payal also told the bus attendant to keep an eye out.

Day 10, the next Wednesday: One of the older boys leaned over on the bus and started to say something. The driver glanced in the mirror. The boy sat back.

Arnab got off at school and walked in with Irfan. His shoulders felt looser than they had in weeks.

qa.q: Where would Arnab sit on the bus under the plan?
qa.a: In the second seat, behind the driver, not the back.

qa.q: What do Arnab's looser shoulders on day 10 suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he felt safer and more relaxed, some of his fear easing once the plan was working.

qa.q: What else could Ms. Payal add to the plan?
qa.a: She could set a weekly check-in with Arnab to see whether the bullying has moved to a new place, so the plan can change too.

qa.q: How might Irfan and Tenzing see their part in the plan?
qa.a: They probably feel trusted and useful, since walking with Arnab is simple but clearly helps him feel safe.

grounding: Shows a student and counsellor identifying bullying hotspots like the bus and a corridor and arranging to walk with friends, sit near staff and know whom to approach.

passage:
Yamini, your Vinita nani wants to tell you something, since you said a girl keeps bothering you on the school van.

When I was fourteen, in Bhopal, a group of older girls cornered me every day by the water tank and in the back of the school tonga. Pinching, snatching my tiffin. I dreaded every morning.

I finally told Sister Agnes, our school counsellor. She didn't just say "be brave". She took out a paper and asked, "Where exactly? When?" We made a plan like a map. In the tonga, I would sit up front beside the driver. At the water tank, I'd go only with my friends Shobha and Rukhsana. And if anything happened, I'd go straight to the staff room.

It didn't stop in a day. But it stopped. Now come. We'll tell your Amma right now, and call your class teacher together this evening.

qa.q: Where did young Vinita sit in the tonga under the plan?
How did young Vinita feel before telling Sister Agnes?
qa.a: She felt frightened and full of dread, afraid of every morning.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why?
qa.a: The turning point was Sister Agnes asking exactly where and when; that turned a vague fear into a map of places and people, instead of just telling her to be brave.

qa.q: How might Shobha and Rukhsana have felt walking with her to the water tank?
qa.a: They likely felt protective and proud to help, since their company made the older girls less likely to target her.

grounding: An elder recalls working with a counsellor to identify where bullying happened and arranging to sit near staff and walk with friends.
